abstract: |
  The [fin-selection study](../fin-selection/) found NACA 0007 with a 100 mm chord the best of the
  symmetric NACA sections. This study asks whether a section from outside that family does better at
  the same chord and the same bending stiffness. XFOIL screened 28 published and modified sections,
  an optimiser searched a family of smooth shapes, and about 330 2D CFD simulations checked the
  leaders. **Answer from the 2D simulations:** Mark Drela's HT35, scaled to 7.25\ % thick, beats
  NACA 0007/100 at every boat speed and every load tested. It saves 0.66\ % of race time in calm
  water (0.38\ % with the resistance slope doubled), about 2.8 boat lengths per race. **Main
  caveat:** the gain depends on how disturbed the water is. It halves at 1\ % turbulence and is gone
  at 2\ %, and nobody has measured a pond's turbulence. It is also a 2D result, smaller than the 2D
  model's uncertainty in absolute drag.

## The question {#sec-question}

The fin-selection study compared symmetric NACA four-digit sections, 6–12\ % thick, and chose NACA 0007
at 100 mm chord (0007/100). Those sections are one family with one shape rule: the thickest point is
always 30\ % of the chord back, and the nose radius follows from the thickness. Sections designed for
low Reynolds numbers, as on model gliders, distribute their thickness differently. Could one of them,
or a new shape, do better on an IOM fin?

The comparison is kept fair in two ways:

* **Same chord, 100 mm.** Only the section shape changes. Every number on this page is at 100 mm.
* **Same bending stiffness.** A section that is thinner where it matters would be faster and softer.
  So each candidate is scaled to the smallest thickness at which its bending stiffness matches
  NACA 0007/100's: HT35 needs 7.25\ % instead of its 7\ %. The
  [fin-selection page](../fin-selection/#sec-conclusion) explains why stiffness matters for holding
  the bulb.

Everything else is as on the fin-selection page: 2D simulations of a horizontal slice of the fin,
the race-time comparison at three side-force loads plus the downwind leg, and the results at three
boat speeds, 0.75, 1 and 1.5 m/s (light air, medium and fresh).

## The sections {#sec-shapes}

![NACA 0007, HT35 at 7.25\ % and cst-opt2, the optimiser's best shape, all at 100 mm chord. At true
scale (top) they are hard to tell apart; the differences are a few tenths of a millimetre. HT35 is
thickest further forward, fuller over the first 40\ % of the chord and thinner behind, and has a
rounder nose and a straighter tail. Drawn from the coordinates used for the
simulations.](../_generated/custom-shapes.svg){#fig-shapes}

[Scroll the table sideways →]{.table-hint}

::: {#tbl-properties}
{{< include ../_generated/custom-properties.md >}}

The three sections at 100 mm chord. Bending stiffness is relative to NACA 0007/100, for a solid
section and for a thin skin over a core. Thickness positions are from the leading edge.
:::

**HT35** is one of Mark Drela's HT sections, from the UIUC airfoil coordinate database
[@uiuc-coords]. As published it is 7\ % thick; here every ordinate is scaled by 7.25/7. Against
NACA 0007 at 100 mm it:

* is thickest at 26 mm instead of 30 mm;
* is up to 0.26 mm fuller on each side over the first 40 mm, and up to 0.25 mm thinner on each side
  from there to the tail;
* has a 0.74 mm nose radius against 0.54 mm, and a 7.1° trailing edge against 9.7°.

**cst-opt2** is the optimiser's best shape (@sec-method). It has the same forward crest and thinner
rear as HT35, NACA 0007's nose radius, and a fuller tail with a 10.4° trailing edge.

**The coordinates** are in the repository:
[`geometry/foils/ht35-t0725.dat`](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/geometry/foils/ht35-t0725.dat),
as a fraction of the chord. That file has 7 decimals, which is ample for the shape but not for reading
the nose radius back from it. For a mould or CAD, export it at 10 decimals with
`python -m iomcfd.sectiondesign export "file:ht35.dat@0.0725"`.

## How the section was found {#sec-method}

The work went in five steps, from fast and rough to slow and careful. The CFD is the same as on the
[fin-selection page](../fin-selection/#sec-method), with one change: angles of 3° and 5° were added
to 0, 2, 4 and 6°.

1. **XFOIL screen.** XFOIL [@drela1989] computes a section's polar in about a second. It was first
   checked against the project's CFD on the seven NACA finalists, and ranked them almost as the CFD
   does, provided the angles are spaced 0.5° apart (rank correlation about 0.9). Then it screened 28
   sections: published low-Reynolds-number sections scaled to 7\ %, and NACA 0007 with a rounder or
   sharper nose and its crest further forward or aft.
2. **CFD screen.** The seven most informative went into steady CFD, 126 simulations: the leaders, and
   tests of what XFOIL might get wrong (a sharp nose, a round nose on NACA 0007, a laminar 6-series
   section).
3. **Optimiser.** XFOIL inside an optimiser (differential evolution, 2460 shapes) searched a family
   of smooth symmetric shapes (CST [@kulfan2008], five shape parameters). Every shape was scaled to
   NACA 0007/100's stiffness. The nose could not be sharper than NACA 0007's, where XFOIL and the CFD
   disagree. The score was the worst case over calm and disturbed water and both resistance slopes.
   Two optima went into the CFD: cst-opt1, with a steep "boat-tail" trailing edge, and cst-opt2,
   with the trailing-edge angle capped at 10.5°.
4. **Time-accurate check.** At 2–5° the flow on these thin sections sheds vortices, and the steady
   solver gets it wrong (as on the [fin-selection page](../fin-selection/#sec-transient)). So
   NACA 0007, HT35 at 7.25\ % and cst-opt2 were run time-accurately at 2, 3, 4 and 5° at all three
   speeds: 20 flow-throughs, averaged over the last 8.
5. **Turbulence check.** The same three sections at Tu 1\ % and 2\ %, steady: there the flow
   settles, and steady results can be trusted.

**Why 3° and 5°.** The race time reads each section's angle and drag at the required side force by
straight lines between the computed angles. Near 0–4° the curves bend, and a 2° grid misplaces the
working load. Leaving out the 3° and 5° points reordered the CFD screen by up to 0.46\ % of race time,
as much as the whole spread of the NACA finalists. This applies to the fin-selection rankings too,
which use a 2° grid; how much it moves them is not yet known.

## Results {#sec-results}

Click any chart to see it larger.

### The steady screen {#sec-screen}

![The steady CFD screen at Tu 0.1\ %: race time gained against NACA 0007, mean of three speeds and
three loads. Bars use the estimated resistance slope; ticks use it doubled. HT35 at 7\ % gains most
but is 7\ % less stiff; at equal stiffness (7.25\ %) it is level with
cst-opt2.](../_generated/custom-screen.svg){#fig-screen}

* **HT35 and cst-opt2 lead,** level with each other within the steady solver's error.
* **Ruled out, in XFOIL and the CFD alike:**
  * a rounder nose on NACA 0007 (NACA 0007-73, 0.4\ % slower);
  * a laminar 6-series section (NACA 64-007, 1.5\ % slower), and thickness further aft;
  * cst-opt1's steep boat-tail. XFOIL credited it with 0.59\ % but the CFD found 0.16\ %: it is the
    one feature where XFOIL misled the optimiser.
* SD8020, with a sharp nose, also beat NACA 0007 (by 0.33\ %); it was not taken further.

These are steady solutions of a flow that sheds at 2–5°, so the screen only chose what to check
time-accurately.

### The gain {#sec-gain}

![Race time gained against NACA 0007/100. Left: by boat speed, in calm water (Tu 0.1\ %), with
time-accurate points at 2–5°. Right: the mean over the three speeds at three levels of water
turbulence; Tu 1 and 2\ % are steady. Bars use the estimated resistance slope, ticks use it doubled.
The right axis converts to boat lengths per race: about 4 per 1\ % (an
estimate).](../_generated/custom-gain.svg){#fig-gain}

[Scroll the table sideways →]{.table-hint}

::: {#tbl-gain}
{{< include ../_generated/custom-gain.md >}}

Race time gained against NACA 0007/100, % (positive = faster): estimated resistance slope / doubled.
Columns 0.75–1.5 m/s and the mean are at Tu 0.1\ %, each the mean of the low, working and high load.
"Least favourable point" is the smallest gain at any of the nine speed and load combinations
(estimated slope). The Tu 1 and 2\ % columns are means over all nine.
:::

* **HT35 at 7.25\ % is ahead at every speed and every load,** by 0.41\ % in light air, 0.71\ % at
  1 m/s and 0.86\ % in fresh air. Even its least favourable point gains 0.21\ %.
* **cst-opt2 is second,** about 0.1\ % behind HT35. At two points it is level with NACA 0007 or a
  little behind. The optimiser's XFOIL score and the CFD disagree in detail.
* **What the time-accurate points changed.** In the steady screen HT35's gain was at 0.75 and
  1 m/s (0.87 and 0.86\ %) with little at 1.5 m/s (0.35\ %). With the time-accurate points the gain
  moved to 1.5 m/s. The mean barely moved: 0.69\ % steady, 0.66\ % time-accurate.

**Fresh air and the two flows on NACA 0007.** At 4° and 1.5 m/s the model finds two flows on
NACA 0007/100, depending on how the simulation starts
([fin-selection](../fin-selection/#sec-by-speed)). The numbers here use the flow found from rest, as
the fin-selection page does. With the other, higher-drag flow HT35's gain at 1.5 m/s would be 1.34\ %
instead of 0.86\ %. Whether HT35 has a second flow too was not tested.

### Calm or disturbed water {#sec-turbulence}

The water's turbulence, Tu, sets how long the boundary layer stays laminar. Nobody has measured it on
a model-yacht pond: a towing tank is under 0.1\ %, and open water is probably 0.5–2\ % (an estimate).

* **Tu 0.1\ % (calm):** 0.66 / 0.38\ % (estimated / doubled resistance slope).
* **Tu 1\ %:** 0.34 / 0.20\ %. The steady solutions settle here (HT35's drag varies by at most 0.6\ %
  between iterations), so no time-accurate check is needed.
* **Tu 2\ % (rough):** break-even on average, 0.01 / 0.00\ %. In light and medium air HT35 still
  gains about 0.5\ % at the high load and loses 0.1–0.2\ % at the working load. In fresh air it
  loses 0.2–0.5\ % at every load: its drag at 0° is now 3\ % above NACA 0007's.

HT35's advantage comes from its laminar boundary layer (@sec-where), and turbulent water takes that
away. On average it is never worse than NACA 0007, so changing to it is a low-risk change: something
to gain in calm water, little to lose in rough.

### Where the gain comes from {#sec-where}

![HT35's gain split as the race-time method adds it up, in calm water (Tu 0.1\ %): less drag upwind
at the same side force, less leeway for that side force, and less drag downwind at
0°.](../_generated/custom-breakdown.svg){#fig-breakdown}

Averaged over all speeds and loads, about half of the 0.66\ % is upwind drag (0.32\ %), a third is
downwind drag (0.24\ %) and a sixth is leeway (0.10\ %). Upwind, the gain is not at the working load:

![Upwind, at equal side force: drag (top) and angle of attack (bottom) of HT35 at 7.25\ % and cst-opt2
against NACA 0007, per boat speed. Below zero is better. The dotted lines are the three loads. The
points at 2–5° are time-accurate, 0° and 6° steady; the lines join them as the ranking does, so
their kinks are at computed
points.](../_generated/custom-upwind.svg){#fig-upwind}

* **At the high load** HT35 has 2.6–4.5\ % less drag. At 5° it makes 4\ % more lift than NACA 0007 with
  2–5\ % less drag.
* **At the working load** the two are level, within 1\ % in drag and 0.06° in angle. The flows at 4°
  look alike too (@fig-flow-4deg-naca, @fig-flow-4deg-ht35).
* **At the low load** HT35 needs less angle: 0.61° against 1.01° at 1 m/s. Near 2° NACA 0007 loses
  lift (@sec-flow); HT35 doesn't. At 1.5 m/s it also has 5\ % less drag there.
* **Downwind,** at 0°, HT35 has 1.8\ % (0.75 m/s) to 4.6\ % (1.5 m/s) less drag, from less skin
  friction (@fig-friction).

### The flow {#sec-flow}

**Downwind, 0°.**

![NACA 0007 and HT35 at 0°, 1 m/s, Tu 0.1\ %, steady. Left: pressure along the surface (above zero,
the water moves faster than the boat). Middle: skin friction. Right: friction drag added up from the
nose, both sides. HT35's water speeds up more over the front and less over the back, and over the
back 70\ % it rubs less. Its friction drag is 5\ % lower; its pressure drag is the same
(C~d~ 0.0030).](../_generated/custom-friction.svg){#fig-friction}

On both sections the boundary layer stays laminar almost to the trailing edge at 0°. HT35's crest is
further forward, so the water slows down earlier and more gently over its thinner back half. A
slower laminar boundary layer has less friction. On NACA 0007 the flow separates very near the
trailing edge (from 94\ % of the chord); on HT35 only at the last half-percent. That costs little
here; the friction is what differs.

**Low load, 2°: lift lost near 0°.** The colours are those of the
[fin-selection gallery](../fin-selection/#sec-gallery): pale is the free stream, dark the slow water
near the wall, blue reversed flow. Each picture is one instant of a time-accurate run, not an average.

![NACA 0007, 100 mm, 2°, 1 m/s, Tu 0.1\ %, time-accurate, one instant. The laminar boundary layer
on the suction side separates at about 70\ % of the chord, and the separated layer reattaches only
at about 94\ %, with a pocket of reversed flow at the trailing edge. A long bubble at the back of
the suction side costs lift: C~l~ 0.127 (time average), C~d~ 0.0122.](../assets/custom-flow-2deg-naca0007.png){#fig-flow-2deg-naca}

![HT35 at 7.25\ %, the same conditions. The boundary layer separates earlier, at about 62\ %, but the
separated layer rolls up into vortices (the two blue pockets) and reattaches by about 79\ %, before
separating again at 85\ %. C~l~ 0.209 (65\ % more, time average), C~d~ 0.0125.](../assets/custom-flow-2deg-ht35.png){#fig-flow-2deg-ht35}

The 2° time-accurate runs are the least certain part of the comparison. HT35's lift there swings by
about 20\ % and was still drifting after 20 flow-throughs. The mechanism, a separated layer that
closes before the trailing edge or not, is the same one the fin-selection page shows for thick
sections in light air ([lift lost near 0°](../fin-selection/#fig-flow-lift-loss)).

**Working load, 4°: much the same.**

![NACA 0007, 100 mm, 4°, 1 m/s, Tu 0.1\ %, time-accurate, one instant. A short laminar bubble near the
leading edge, then vortices travelling along the rear half (the blue pockets). C~l~ 0.399, C~d~ 0.0140
(time averages).](../assets/custom-flow-4deg-naca0007.png){#fig-flow-4deg-naca}

![HT35 at 7.25\ %, the same conditions. The same pattern; the first bubble starts a little later
(about 13\ % of the chord, against 7\ %). C~l~ 0.405, C~d~ 0.0142.](../assets/custom-flow-4deg-ht35.png){#fig-flow-4deg-ht35}

## Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

*Everything here comes from 2D simulations of the fin section, not from tests of a fin. Confidence in
the answer is medium, for the reasons below.*

**Recommended: HT35 scaled to 7.25\ % thickness, at 100 mm chord.** This replaces the section of the
fin-selection page's answer, NACA 0007/100; the chord stays at 100 mm, the only chord tested here.

* **It is as stiff in bending as NACA 0007/100,** 0.25 mm thicker, with its thickness further
  forward.
* **In calm water it saves 0.66\ % of race time** (0.38\ % with the resistance slope doubled), about
  2.8 boat lengths per race (1.6), and it is ahead at every speed and load tested.
* **In moderately disturbed water (Tu 1\ %)** it saves about half that; **in rough water (Tu 2\ %)**
  it breaks even.
* **cst-opt2**, the optimiser's shape, comes second, about 0.1\ % behind. It is not a published
  section and has no advantage over HT35, so it is not recommended.

**How much is at stake.** About 0.4–0.7\ % of race time in calm water, 2–3 boat lengths per race.
That is similar to what the choice between the best NACA sections was worth, and smaller than the 2D
model's uncertainty in absolute drag. A dirty or unfair fin can cost as much (see the
[fin-selection conclusion](../fin-selection/#sec-conclusion)).

**Why the confidence is not higher:**

* **The model.** The transition model was checked against one section at one Reynolds number, and
  its weak spot is separation bubbles. The ranking assumes its errors are similar for similar
  sections; no measurement confirms that for these shapes.
* **The water.** The gain depends on Tu, which hasn't been measured on a pond, and the model
  represents pond turbulence by one number.
* **The least certain points.** The 2° points, where much of the leeway gain comes from, oscillate
  and drift. 0° and 6° are steady solutions.
* **2D, constant chord.** Tip, bulb, hull junction, heel and taper are not modelled.
* **Estimated inputs,** as on the fin-selection page: the resistance slope and the course.

**What would change it:**

* a 3D simulation of HT35 at 7.25\ % on a tapered fin against NACA 0007 on the same planform;
* whether HT35 also has a second, higher-drag flow at 1.5 m/s, as NACA 0007 does;
* a check of how accurately a mould must follow the coordinates (XFOIL suggests errors of 0.05 mm
  cost little);
* a tow test or two boats sailing side by side.

## The studies, one by one (click to open)

::: {#tbl-studies}
| when | study | question | answer |
|:----|:----------------|:----------------|:------------------------|
| 18\ Oct | XFOIL calibration | Does XFOIL rank sections as the project's CFD does? | Yes on 0.5° steps (rank correlation 0.89–0.96); it misses the CFD's penalty on sharp noses. On the 2° grid it ranks them wrongly. |
| 18\ Oct | XFOIL screen: 28 sections | Which published or modified sections beat NACA 0007? | SD8020, E168, HT35 and HT34 at 7\ %. A rounder nose alone, or thickness further aft, doesn't help. |
| 18\ Oct | optimiser: 2460 shapes in XFOIL | Can a new shape do better at equal stiffness? | Two optima, both of HT35's family: crest at 25\ %, fuller front, thinner middle. |
| 18\ Oct | CFD screen: 7 sections; 126 cases | Do the XFOIL leaders hold in CFD? | HT35 beats NACA 0007 at every speed. XFOIL ranks the seven exactly as the steady CFD does. |
| 18\ Oct | CFD optima: 54 cases | And the optimiser's shapes? | cst-opt2 is level with HT35; cst-opt1's boat-tail doesn't pay. |
| 18\ Oct | Tu 1 and 2\ %: 108 cases | What if the water is more disturbed? | The gain halves at Tu 1\ % and is gone at 2\ %. The flow is steady there. |
| 18–21\ Oct | time-accurate check: 36 cases, 7 again after Spot VMs were lost, 3 reruns | Does the gain hold when the shedding is resolved? | Yes, at every speed and load. HT35 first, cst-opt2 second. |
| 23\ Oct | analysis | NACA 0007 started from rest at 1.5 m/s | HT35's gain revised from 0.82\ % to 0.66\ %. |

## Reproducing this {.appendix .unnumbered}

Everything is in [the repository](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd): the simulation setup
(`projects/foil2d/`), every study file, the section coordinates (`geometry/foils/`), the XFOIL
wrapper and the section tools (`src/iomcfd/xfoil.py`, `src/iomcfd/sectiondesign.py`), and the
findings log with the numbers behind each conclusion. This page's charts are drawn from the small
data files below, which `iomcfd site export` copies out of the runs; the race times are computed
from them with the same code (`sectiondesign.cfd_table` and `rank`) that produced the findings. The
flow pictures are ParaView renders (`iomcfd viz`) of the few cases fetched whole. The code is under
the [MIT licence](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/LICENSE); the text, figures and data
on this page are under CC BY 4.0. The HT35 coordinates come from the UIUC database and keep its terms.
